solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What may lead animal who's reluctant to move?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rope and headstall used to lead a horse or cow
second meaning: one who halts, stopping rather than going on

explanation.surface: A stubborn beast being coaxed along: what gets it moving?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one question about a balky animal, but it splits into two: the harness that leads it, and a whimsical 'one who halts'.
explanation.definitionFit: A halter is the headgear used for leading livestock, and the second sense is a playful agent noun built from the verb meaning to stop.

clue.text: Test starts late enough for everyone

indicators.note: beginning late means the opening letter is missed out

parts.note: to sample something is to test or try it

explanation.surface: An exam that begins behind schedule but runs long enough for all the candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts late' looks like a timing problem with the exam; read it as 'start missing', so SAMPLE loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ample is plentiful, more than sufficient, so there is enough to go round all the people present.

clue.text: Virago books extends title range

parts.note: a title is a name or term of address
an Aga is a brand of kitchen range, the cast-iron cooker
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Virago, the publisher, grows its range of titles.
explanation.walkthrough: Virago looks like the feminist publishing house, which makes 'books' and 'title range' feel like a catalogue; the books are NT, which extends (is added to the end of) TERM and AGA. An Aga is a British cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are old names for a fierce, bullying, overbearing woman, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Wreckage of buildings caused by King intially breaking law

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a rule is a law or regulation
the blues guitarist B.B. King is known by his initials

explanation.surface: A monarch flouting the law has left buildings in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King initially' looks like an instruction to take K; instead it means King's initials, as in the bluesman B.B. King. (The clue's 'intially' is the printed spelling.)
explanation.definitionFit: Rubble is the broken stone and brick left when structures collapse or are demolished, so it is the debris of destroyed houses.

clue.text: Fairly strong bouts of illness held back members of school

indicators.note: something held back is turned around and sent the other way

parts.note: fits are sudden attacks or bouts of illness
a school is a shoal, so its members are fish

explanation.surface: Pupils kept off by repeated bouts of sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' suggests pupils kept back a year; here it is a school of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The -ish suffix means somewhat, so a rather stiff breeze or drink is moderately powerful or forceful.

clue.text: Gaffe that may make it difficult to get into Oxford

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a word said by mistake

definitions.text: that may make it difficult to get into Oxford
definitions.note: a fanciful description of a shoe problem rather than a dictionary sense
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an Oxford is a lace-up shoe, and if the flap under its laces slides out of place the foot will not go in

explanation.surface: A blunder at interview that might cost an applicant a place at Oxford University.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the university and the gaffe like an interview howler; it is the Oxford shoe, whose tongue may slip.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the idiom for an inadvertent verbal error, saying something you did not mean to say.

clue.text: Masculine way of working stopping that is not right

definitions.note: in the sense of not proper or decorous

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the plug sits inside the opening

parts.note: id est is the Latin behind the abbreviation i.e.
M is the grammatical abbreviation for masculine
MO is modus operandi, a way of working

explanation.surface: A macho working style that halts what is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' is usually IE; here the full Latin ID EST is needed, plugged between its I and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Immodest behaviour is indecorous or improper, the opposite of what is fitting and seemly in polite company.

clue.text: University dons shape discussion

indicators.note: to don is to put on, as a garment wraps the wearer

parts.note: form is shape or outline
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Academics steering a debate at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like a noun for university lecturers; it is the verb 'puts on', so FORM wears U.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a meeting or medium where ideas are exchanged and debated, so it can stand for the debate itself.

clue.text: Richness of incentive securing advance orders to begin with

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so one part is gripped inside another

parts.note: a spur is an incentive or stimulus
to advance money is to lend it

indicators.note: only the very start of the word is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lucrative bonus scheme tied to early orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The business picture of orders paid in advance is a disguise: 'advance' is the verb for handing over a loan, not prepayment.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendour is magnificence, lavish grandeur and opulence, which is the sense of richness in decor or display.

clue.text: Sportsman who's paid by Britain embroiled in drug shame

indicators.note: to be embroiled in something is to be caught up inside it

parts.note: opium is a narcotic drug
a professional is paid to play
BR is an abbreviation for Britain

explanation.surface: A British-funded athlete caught up in a doping scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: The doping story fits the surface neatly, but the drug is an old narcotic rather than a performance enhancer, and 'paid' marks a professional as opposed to an amateur.
explanation.definitionFit: Opprobrium is public disgrace or harsh criticism resulting from bad conduct, a close synonym for ignominy.

clue.text: Bank is genuinely heartless

indicators.note: without a heart means the centre of the word is cut away

parts.note: really means genuinely or truly

explanation.surface: A complaint that a bank truly has no compassion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like the financial institution of the surface; it is the verb, as in to bank on someone. REALLY loses its middle AL.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to count on or depend on them, which is what relying means.

clue.text: Almost all orgies affected wives collectively

indicators.note: nearly the whole thing means its last letter is dropped
something affected is altered or disturbed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word with its final letter cut
taken as written

explanation.surface: Debauched parties had an effect on nearly all the married women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost all' reads as a quantity of orgies; it is the instruction to trim ALL to AL before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraglio is a harem, the women's quarters of a household, and by extension the group of wives and concubines kept there.

clue.text: Reduce staff employed in key market

parts.note: to deman is to cut the manpower of a business
D is a musical key

explanation.surface: Cutting the workforce in a crucial market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key market' looks like a single phrase; key is the musical D and market is the definition. DEMAN is a rare dictionary verb meaning to cut staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A market for goods is the appetite of buyers for them, which economists call demand.

clue.text: Petition bound to bring pressure to the fore

indicators.text: to bring pressure to the fore
indicators.note: bringing something to the fore moves it from the back up to the front of the word

parts.note: a bound is a leap or jump

explanation.surface: A petition that is certain to push an issue up the agenda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to'; bound is a noun, LEAP, and its final P (the physics symbol for pressure) moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea is an earnest request or appeal, the same as a petition made to someone in authority.

clue.text: Period of consumption lent one much to work on

indicators.note: material to work on is raw stuff to be reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lent gave someone a great deal to get on with, as if Lent were a period of self-denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Period' and 'Lent' together suggest the fasting season, and 'consumption' could be tuberculosis; the definition is just a time for eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunchtime is the midday interval when people eat, so it is literally a time span of eating food.

clue.text: Corrupt state cut down politician who has good will?

indicators.note: corrupted text is garbled, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: cutting something down shortens it by its last letter

parts.note: a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A crooked regime has toppled a well-meaning politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good will' sounds like benevolence; the question mark points to a legal will, the document a testator leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator is a person who has made a valid will disposing of their estate, so they literally possess a sound will.

clue.text: Plant belonging to boring drinking establishment

indicators.note: something boring drills its way into the inside of another thing

parts.note: an auberge is an inn, from the French
to be in a club or group is to belong to it

explanation.surface: A pot plant that belongs to a dull pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like 'dull', describing the pub; it means drilling into. The French word for an inn is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The aubergine, called eggplant in America, is a plant of the nightshade family grown for its purple fruit.

clue.text: Cherish silence preserved by inner circle's last broadcast

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters seed far and wide, so the letters are strewn about

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
taken as written

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is the one wanted

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A secret kept by a powerful clique is finally made public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inner circle' looks like one phrase; the words split, with INNER whole and only the end of 'circle' used.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshrine something is to treasure it and keep it as sacred, which is a way of holding it dear.

clue.text: Popular point of view for example

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a stance is a position or attitude on an issue

explanation.surface: A widely held opinion offered by way of illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' reads as a single phrase; split off 'for' and the definition is 'example', echoing the idiom 'for instance'.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case cited to illustrate something, which is what an example means.

clue.text: Writer's brief life story about queen

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed around another

parts.note: bio is the short form of biography
R is for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: An author's short biography of a royal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' looks like an author, the subject of the life story; it is a pen. Biro is the British everyday word for a ballpoint pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A Biro is a ballpoint pen, and in crosswords a writer is often an instrument used for writing rather than a person.

clue.text: Reluctant to admit support from military planes has lowered resistance

definitions.note: as in 'I'm afraid', said before an unwelcome admission

indicators.note: in a down entry, lowering a symbol for an electrical property moves it from the top of its word to the bottom

parts.note: the RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force
aid is support or help

explanation.surface: Someone loath to concede that air cover has weakened the defence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lowered resistance' sounds like weakened defences, but R is the symbol for electrical resistance, and in this down entry it drops from the top of its word to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I'm afraid' is the polite preface to confessing something unwelcome, showing hesitancy about owning up.

clue.text: Punish worthless people injecting heroin

indicators.note: injecting puts something inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: trash is a contemptuous word for worthless people
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A call to penalise lowlifes who shoot up heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug-user scene makes 'injecting' literal, but it simply puts H into TRASH.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrash someone is to beat them hard, typically as chastisement, so it is a forceful way to discipline.

clue.text: Place hosting final of competition?

indicators.note: a host has guests within, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: an area is a place or region
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Where would a cup final be staged?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: AREA hosts the last letter of 'competition', and an arena is where a final is staged.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a stadium or enclosed venue for sporting contests, exactly where a cup final would be held.

clue.text: Proposal from further education syndicate

parts.note: off can mean farther away, as in the off side of a horse or road
E is an abbreviation for education
a ring is a group or cartel acting together

explanation.surface: A plan put forward by a group of colleges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Further education' reads as one phrase meaning post-school colleges (FE); split them, with 'further' as OFF and 'education' as E.
explanation.definitionFit: An offering is something put forward for acceptance, like a suggestion or bid, which matches a proposal.

clue.text: What may be used as fertiliser, given it replenishes borders

definitions.text: What may be used as fertiliser

indicators.note: the answer lies along the borders where neighbouring words meet, straddling them

parts.note: the letters run across the ends and starts of these words

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: use this as plant food, since it restores the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borders' looks like garden flower beds, fitting the fertiliser surface; it is the signal that the answer crosses word boundaries.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre is potassium nitrate, saltpetre, a nitrogen-rich salt long applied to soil to feed crops.

clue.text: Assistant's cyclical adjustment to plan

indicators.note: a cyclical change rotates the letters round, moving the end to the start

parts.note: an idea is a plan or scheme

explanation.surface: A helper's routine tweak to a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: IDEA's last letter moves round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide is a helper or right-hand person to someone senior, the same role as an assistant.

clue.text: Get into good books treating AI differently

indicators.note: doing things differently means a new order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: How to win favour: handle artificial intelligence in a new way.
explanation.walkthrough: AI looks like artificial intelligence, a topical surface; it is just two letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingratiate oneself is to win someone's favour deliberately, which is the idiom of earning a place in their good books.

clue.text: Incomprehensible language one's subjected to at the bar?

parts.words: one's subjected to at the bar?
parts.note: surface reading: the slurred talk a drinker endures in a pub
setter's reading: the bar is the legal profession, whose jargon baffles laymen

explanation.surface: The baffling chatter you must put up with at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar looks like a pub counter; it is the courtroom bar, the legal profession, whose jargon is notoriously opaque.
explanation.definitionFit: Legalese is the dense, technical jargon of lawyers and statutes, famously hard for ordinary readers to follow.

clue.text: Want backing to include games at school and change pitch

indicators.note: backing up means going in the opposite direction
including something takes it in, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: to want is to need
PE is physical education, school games lessons

explanation.surface: Wanting backing to bring school sport in and change the playing field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a sports field, in keeping with the games; it is the pitch of a sound or voice.
explanation.definitionFit: When a voice or note deepens it becomes lower in tone, so its musical frequency alters downward.
